description: How Senator McCarthy made Communist subversion the dominant theme of US politics 1950–1954.
content_html:
The Rise of Senator McCarthy

On 9 February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin spoke at a Republican women’s club in Wheeling, West Virginia. He claimed to be holding a list of 205 members of the Communist Party who were “still working and shaping policy in the State Department.” The precise number varied every time he repeated the claim, but the accusation landed at exactly the right moment — Alger Hiss had just been convicted, the Soviet Union had just tested its first atomic bomb, and China had just ‘fallen’ to Communism. McCarthyism had begun.

Key Fact

McCarthy delivered his Wheeling speech in February 1950, claiming to hold a list of Communists working inside the State Department. The number on the list shifted between speeches, but the charge — that traitors occupied the heart of American government — gripped the nation.

Why McCarthy Had Support

McCarthy was not working alone, and his support came from varied sources. Republican politicians who had spent nearly 20 years out of presidential power saw anti-Communism as a way to attack the Democrats. Business conservatives resented the New Deal and portrayed government regulation as a step towards socialism. Many ordinary Americans were genuinely frightened by the external events of 1949–50. Religious groups saw Communism as an atheist threat to Christian America. McCarthy tapped into all of these currents.

His methods were distinctive. He made sweeping accusations without presenting verifiable evidence. When challenged, he would shift his claims. He called critics of his methods Communist sympathisers, making it dangerous to oppose him publicly. The Democratic-controlled Tydings Committee investigated his original charges in 1950 and concluded they were a “fraud and a hoax,” but McCarthy attacked the committee’s chairman and the report made little impact.

McCarthyism’s most lasting damage was economic and social. People named as Communist sympathisers — teachers, writers, civil servants, scientists, academics — lost their jobs, often without any opportunity to challenge the accusations. The blacklist operated in Hollywood, the civil service and universities. People were dismissed not for proven crimes but for past memberships, attendance at meetings, or association with named individuals. Some emigrated to Europe; others committed suicide. The scale of personal destruction was enormous.

Opposition to McCarthy

Not everyone was silent. Edward R. Murrow, the CBS journalist, produced two landmark television programmes in March 1954 on his show See It Now, using McCarthy’s own words and footage to show viewers how he worked — the interruptions, the unsubstantiated claims, the attacks on witnesses’ patriotism. Murrow’s conclusion was pointed: “We must not confuse dissent with disloyalty.” The programmes shifted public opinion significantly.

McCarthy’s downfall came when he turned on the US Army, claiming in early 1954 that it was harbouring Communists. The Army fought back. Televised hearings ran from April to June 1954. Joseph Welch, the Army’s lead counsel, delivered the most memorable line of the era. When McCarthy attacked a young lawyer in Welch’s firm, Welch said quietly: “Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?” The hearing room applauded. Millions watching on television saw McCarthy for what he was. In December 1954 the Senate voted 67–22 to censure him for conduct unbecoming a senator. His power evaporated. He died in May 1957.

Key Fact

Two figures broke McCarthy’s hold: journalist Edward R. Murrow, whose televised ‘See It Now’ programmes exposed McCarthy’s methods in March 1954; and Army counsel Joseph Welch, whose “Have you no sense of decency?” rebuke at the Army-McCarthy hearings ended McCarthy’s public support.

McCarthyism and Broader Anti-Communism

It is important to understand that McCarthyism was extreme even within its era. Mainstream anti-Communism — supporting Truman’s Loyalty Order, backing NATO, opposing Soviet expansion — had wide bipartisan support and was a reasonable response to genuine Soviet threats. McCarthyism went further: it used unsubstantiated accusation, bypassed due process and used fear to silence legitimate dissent. The distinction matters for understanding why McCarthy eventually lost support: most Americans could be anti-Communist without endorsing witch-hunts.

The Legacy of McCarthyism

Even after McCarthy’s fall, the damage he had done to American political culture persisted for years. The blacklist in Hollywood continued into the early 1960s. Federal loyalty boards kept operating. People remained reluctant to join organisations or express unorthodox views for fear of being denounced. Some historians argue that McCarthyism permanently narrowed the range of acceptable political speech in America, making it harder to advocate progressive causes without being labelled subversive. Others point out that the institutions ultimately functioned as intended: the Senate censured McCarthy, the free press exposed him, and the courts gradually rolled back the most extreme measures. The debate about the scale of McCarthyism’s long-term damage to American civil liberties remains an active area of historical inquiry.
exam_tip_html: Examiners expect you to distinguish McCarthyism (McCarthy’s Senate campaign, blacklists, unsubstantiated accusations) from the wider anti-Communist consensus of the period. In a question about “the nature and support for McCarthyism,” show you understand why McCarthy had backing (Republican politics, genuine fear, media coverage) as well as why opposition grew (Army-McCarthy hearings, Murrow broadcasts). Date precision matters: Wheeling speech February 1950, censure December 1954. Avoid describing McCarthy as if he was the only source of the Red Scare — HUAC and Hoover predated him.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • McCarthy exploited the anxieties of 1950 — the Soviet bomb, Korea, Hiss — to build a political movement based on accusation rather than evidence, destroying careers and silencing dissent.
  • His support came from Republicans seeking power, business conservatives, religious groups and genuinely frightened Americans; his opposition came from Democrats, journalists and eventually the Army.
  • The Army-McCarthy hearings of 1954 and Murrow’s television programmes turned public opinion; the Senate censured McCarthy in December 1954, ending his influence — but the damage to civil liberties lasted far longer.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Wheeling speech that launched McCarthy's campaign.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Identifies the Wheeling speech (February 1950) and gives specific detail, e.g. McCarthy claimed to hold a list of 205 Communists working in the State Department, though the number varied between speeches. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to McCarthy making accusations. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the methods McCarthy used during his anti-Communist campaign.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) McCarthy made sweeping accusations without verifiable evidence, shifting his claims when challenged; (2) he labelled critics as Communist sympathisers, making it dangerous to oppose him publicly. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why McCarthyism attracted support from different groups in American society in the early 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains support from multiple groups with specific evidence — Republican politicians used anti-Communism to attack Democrats; business conservatives saw it as a weapon against New Deal liberalism; religious groups feared atheist Communism; ordinary Americans were frightened by genuine external threats. Shows how these groups' motivations reinforced each other. Secure: Two or more reasons explained with evidence. Developing: Lists groups without explaining their motivations. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why opposition to McCarthyism grew between 1950 and 1954.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) Edward R. Murrow's 1954 television broadcasts exposed McCarthy's methods to a mass audience, shifting public opinion against him; (2) the Army-McCarthy hearings, broadcast live on television, allowed millions to see McCarthy's bullying style and hear Welch's rebuke, making his support unsustainable. Each reason includes specific evidence and a clear explanation. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence and explanation. Developing: Two reasons identified but limited development. Emerging: One weak reason.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of television in ending McCarthy's political career?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis weighing television against other factors. Television was significant: Murrow's programmes and the live Army-McCarthy hearings let millions judge McCarthy directly; the medium showed his methods rather than just reporting them. But other factors also matter: the Army's willingness to fight back provided the forum; McCarthy's overreach (attacking the Army) alienated Republican allies; the Tydings Committee report and growing Senate opposition existed independently. Integrated judgement about relative significance. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes television's role without weighing it against other factors. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the causes and effects of McCarthyism on American society in the years 1950 to 1954.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering causes (external shocks, political opportunism, genuine fear, institutional mechanisms) and effects (careers destroyed, civil liberties eroded, chilling effect on free speech, political opponents silenced) with well-chosen evidence throughout. Reaches an integrated judgement. Secure: Several causes and effects with evidence; some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited analytical structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

What action did the Senate take against McCarthy in December 1954?

Joseph Welch, the Army's lawyer at the 1954 hearings, challenged McCarthy with the words: "Have you no sense of _____?"

Senator who claimed Communists were in the State Department

flashcard_questions.q: When and where did McCarthy deliver his Wheeling speech?
What claim did McCarthy make at Wheeling?
flashcard_questions.a: That he had a list of Communists working inside the State Department.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Tydings Committee's verdict on McCarthy's charges?
flashcard_questions.a: It called them a 'fraud and a hoax' in 1950 — but McCarthy survived by attacking the chairman.

flashcard_questions.q: What programme did Edward R. Murrow use to challenge McCarthy?
flashcard_questions.a: See It Now, broadcast on CBS in March 1954.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Joseph Welch say to McCarthy at the Army-McCarthy hearings?
flashcard_questions.a: "Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?"

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Senate censure McCarthy?
flashcard_questions.a: December 1954, by a vote of 67 to 22.
An informal list of people suspected of Communist sympathies whose careers in entertainment, media and government were effectively ended.

flashcard_questions.q: How does McCarthyism differ from broader anti-Communism of the 1950s?
flashcard_questions.a: McCarthyism used unsubstantiated accusations and bypassed due process; mainstream anti-Communism had bipartisan support and responded to genuine Soviet threats.

glossary_terms.definition: The political movement, atmosphere of suspicion and tactics associated with Senator Joseph McCarthy's anti-Communist campaign from 1950 to 1954.
An informal list circulated by employers in entertainment, media and government of individuals suspected of Communist sympathies, whose careers were effectively ended.
The chief counsel for the US Army during the 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings, whose rebuke of McCarthy is credited with turning public opinion against him.
A system of government that protects individual rights and freedoms, including free speech, fair trials and political dissent.
